title: Finding Your Customer and Market Fit
description: Learn to define your ideal customer profile, craft a value proposition, and position against competitors.

interactions.prompt: What does ICP stand for in go-to-market strategy?

options.text: Ideal Customer Profile
Internal Company Priority
Integrated Channel Plan
Initial Conversion Point

interactions.teachingPreamble: Before launching a product, companies need to identify exactly who they're selling to. An Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) describes the type of company or person most likely to buy your product and get the most value from it  -  like how Slack initially targeted small tech teams, not entire Fortune 500 companies.

interactions.prompt: A B2B SaaS startup sees these trial-to-paid conversion rates: Companies with 10-50 employees convert at 22%, 51-200 at 8%, 201-1000 at 3%, and 1000+ at 1%. What's the key insight?

options.text: The product is too expensive for large companies
Small companies (10-50 employees) are the strongest ICP
They need more enterprise sales reps
Larger companies just take longer to convert

chartData.title: Trial-to-Paid Conversion Rate by Company Size

interactions.prompt: What is a value proposition primarily designed to communicate?

options.text: A complete list of product features
Why a customer should choose you over alternatives
Your company's mission and vision statement
The price advantage you offer in the market

interactions.teachingPreamble: A value proposition is a clear statement of why a customer should buy from you instead of anyone else. It connects a specific customer pain to your unique solution  -  for example, Zoom's early value prop was dead-simple video calls that 'just work,' directly targeting frustration with buggy competitors like WebEx.

interactions.prompt: A strong value proposition connects a specific customer ____ to your product's unique solution.

options.text: Budget
Pain point
Department
Industry

interactions.prompt: You're launching a project management tool. Asana dominates mid-market teams and Monday.com owns small businesses. You have limited resources. Which positioning move do you make?

options.text: Compete head-to-head with Asana on features
Target an underserved niche like creative agencies
Offer the lowest price to win on cost
Build for enterprise with a large sales team

interactions.prompt: What is the main purpose of competitive positioning?

options.text: Copying the market leader's strategy to reduce risk
Defining how you're meaningfully different in your customers' minds
Listing every competitor's weaknesses in marketing materials
Setting your price lower than every competitor

interactions.teachingPreamble: Competitive positioning is about owning a distinct space in your customer's mind. You don't need to be better at everything  -  you need to be clearly different on what matters most to your ICP. When HubSpot entered the CRM market against Salesforce, they didn't try to out-feature them  -  they positioned as the CRM that's free to start and easy for small marketing teams.

interactions.prompt: You're building a GTM strategy from scratch for a new B2B analytics tool. Rank these steps in the correct order from first to last.

options.text: Craft your value proposition messaging
Define your Ideal Customer Profile
Choose your go-to-market channels
Analyze competitors and find positioning gaps

interactions.prompt: Your top competitor just launched a free tier targeting your exact ICP of small creative agencies. What's your best immediate response?

options.text: Launch your own free tier to match them
Double down on specialized features competitors can't easily copy
Pivot to a completely different customer segment
Lower all your prices by 50% across the board

interactions.priorContext: Earlier you chose to position your project management tool for an underserved niche of creative agencies. Now a well-funded competitor has noticed and is targeting the same niche with a free offering.
